name: Synthetism
summary: Flat areas of pure colour held by a dark outline, painted from memory and feeling. The painter combines the seen scene, the feeling and the pure form of line and colour into one simple, decorative picture.

philosophy.core_thesis: A picture should join the thing seen, the feeling of the painter and the pure form of colour and line, and it should not copy the scene from the eye.
design_principles: Fill each shape with one flat colour and no gradient, in a patch of 30–300mm.
Draw a dark blue or black contour of 3–8mm around every patch, like the lead of a stained-glass window.
Choose colours by feeling and not by nature: a red field, a yellow Christ, a blue tree.
Flatten the space to 2 layers, with no cast shadow and no single-point perspective.
Set the shapes in a rhythm of curves, and cut the scene by a tree or a high horizon at 10–20% from the top.
Paint from memory and from sketches, so that detail is lost and the main form stays.
Choose a simple, devout or rustic subject, such as women at prayer, a field, a calvary or a farm.
anti_patterns: Soft, blended modelling of the form
Atmospheric perspective with a pale far distance
Broken dabs of colour that mix in the eye
Fine, exact detail of the scene
A realistic, local colour copied from nature

composition.layout: A few large flat patches set against a high horizon, joined by curved dark contours, with a tree trunk or a figure that cuts the picture at a diagonal.
composition.focal_point: The strongest colour patch, a red or yellow, placed within the central 40% of the canvas and at one third from an edge.
composition.format: A canvas at 4:5 to 3:2; the figures are large, and the edges crop the scene hard.

principles.rule: Reduce the depth to 2 layers and put the horizon at 10–20% from the top, so that the ground fills the picture.
Set one pure complementary pair, such as red against green, in the focal area with a value gap of 30% or more.
Repeat a curved contour of 3–8mm around 5 or more patches, with each curve echoing its neighbour.
Give the main figure or the central patch 30–50% of the picture area, in the purest colour.
Fill 60–70% of the area with 2 flat colours, 20–30% with a contrast colour, and under 10% with the dark contour.
Leave large empty patches of one flat colour, and put no detail in them.

palette.strategy: Pure, flat colours chosen for feeling: a red ground, a yellow figure, a blue-green tree, all held by a dark blue contour.
palette.distribution: Two dominant flat colours 60–70%, a contrast colour 20–30%, a dark contour under 10%.
palette.ground: A pale, warm ground that shows at the edge of a patch.

brushwork_and_medium.medium: Oil paint, thin and matt, with little medium, laid in even coats.
brushwork_and_medium.support: Rough canvas or coarse sacking, often a small to medium size.
brushwork_and_medium.brushwork: Flat fills with a stroke of 5–15mm that does not show; the visible stroke follows the edge of the patch.
brushwork_and_medium.paint_handling: 1 layer of opaque colour, under 1mm thick; the colour is not blended and no glaze is added.
brushwork_and_medium.edges: A dark blue or black contour of 3–8mm in a smooth curve; the patches meet at the contour.

light_and_modelling.light: None from a source; the light is a pure yellow or a warm white patch.
light_and_modelling.modelling: By a flat change of colour from one patch to the next, with no gradient.
light_and_modelling.shadow: No cast shadow; a form turns by its contour and by a darker patch of the same hue.
light_and_modelling.temperature: Warm patches against cool ones, set side by side at full chroma.

subject.typical: Breton women at prayer or in a field, a calvary, a farm, a tree and a hill, a vision of a scene from the Bible.
subject.figure_scale: A figure fills 40–80% of the picture height, often in a group of 3–6.
subject.treatment: Simple, devout and rustic; the scene is a dream or a memory, and the mood is quiet and strange.

surface.texture: Flat and even, with the weave of the canvas in view.

works.work: Mahana no atua (Day of the God)
No te aha oe riri (Why Are You Angry?)

reference_works.note: Object ids were checked against the Art Institute of Chicago API (CC0 data). All three works are by Gauguin. The Arlésiennes is from the Synthetist years at Pont-Aven and Arles; the other two come from Tahiti, where he kept the method. Look at the museum page for the image and its licence.

emotion.target_response: A quiet, dreamlike intensity: the viewer meets a simple scene made strange by pure colour.

use_cases: poster and label art with flat colour
avoid_when: The brief needs modelled volume, depth or a photographic look.
The picture must show a fine technical detail.

modifiers.how: Keep the strong colour; drop the even fill, show a stroke of 5–15mm that follows the form, and thicken the paint to 2–5mm.
Keep the flat patch and the contour; add a quiet, dreamlike subject, a pale, soft palette and a rhythm of long curves.

sources.title: Art Institute of Chicago API (CC0 data)
Albert Aurier, Le Symbolisme en peinture: Paul Gauguin (Mercure de France, 1891)
